power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Xinkai Du and Sverre Urnes Johnson are supported by Helse Sør-Øst RHF (grant 2022107), which is owned by the Norwegian state through the Ministry of Health and Care.

Although depression and anxiety are distinct diagnostic categories, they often do not present as isolated conditions; instead, they co-occur so frequently that comorbidity, defined here as the presence of more than one diagnosable disorder in the same individual, is a central clinical presentation rather than an exception in clinical populations (Cheng et al., 2025; Lamers et al., 2011; Li et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Although depression and anxiety are distinct diagnostic categories, they often do not present as isolated conditions; instead, they co-occur so frequently that comorbidity, defined here as the presence of more than one diagnosable disorder in the same individual, is a central clinical presentation rather than an exception in clinical populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cheng et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lamers et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Li et al., 2025b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Zhang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety (NESDA), among patients diagnosed with depression, 75% were diagnosed with anxiety at least once in their lifetime, and 67% were currently suffering from an anxiety disorder; among patients diagnosed with anxiety, 63% were suffering from a current depressive disorder, and 81% were diagnosed with a depressive disorder at least once (Lamers et al., 2011).
text.formatted: In the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety (NESDA), among patients diagnosed with depression, 75% were diagnosed with anxiety at least once in their lifetime, and 67% were currently suffering from an anxiety disorder; among patients diagnosed with anxiety, 63% were suffering from a current depressive disorder, and 81% were diagnosed with a depressive disorder at least once <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lamers et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The comorbidity of anxiety and depression has been a major contributor to more persistent or treatment-resistant symptom presentations and a challenge to intervention, linked to greater need for professional care, worse clinical outcomes, more disruption to daily functioning, and elevated suicide risk (Beard et al., 2016; Kaiser et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

text.text: The study of comorbidity and psychology in general was heavily influenced by latent-variable models, such as factor and item-response theory models (Borsboom, 2008; Cramer et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The study of comorbidity and psychology in general was heavily influenced by latent-variable models, such as factor and item-response theory models <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Borsboom, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cramer et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This perspective defines and studies mental disorders as unobservable latent common causes that lead to a series of observable features (i.e., symptoms).
The observed correlations among features arise from the latent common cause.
These correlations are considered trivial and are expected to disappear once the common cause is controlled for (Pearl, 2009).
text.formatted: These correlations are considered trivial and are expected to disappear once the common cause is controlled for <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Pearl, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Remaining correlations among residuals 1 are considered to be violations of the local independence assumption (Kline & Little, 2023).
text.formatted: Remaining correlations among residuals 1 are considered to be violations of the local independence assumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kline & Little, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Treating symptoms themselves or targeting their relations has no impact on the latent common causes, as the symptoms are the effects rather than the cause of mental disorders.

observed correlations among sneezing, headache, and coughing are meaningless, and treating these symptoms themselves does not cure a cold, as the cold itself is a latent common cause (i.e., a virus or bacterial infection).
Curing the cold requires targeting the common cause of the symptoms: the virus or the infection.
Once the common cause is removed, the symptoms will disappear naturally.

Applying such a perspective to psychopathology is challenging: despite extensive research, attempts to identify shared pathogenic mechanisms have not yet produced a clear or consistent answer for most mental disorders (Borsboom et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Applying such a perspective to psychopathology is challenging: despite extensive research, attempts to identify shared pathogenic mechanisms have not yet produced a clear or consistent answer for most mental disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Borsboom et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, symptoms and their correlations are meaningful.
For example, sleep disturbance can lead to lethargy, which can impair concentration.
The latent-variable perspective is also limited in its understanding of comorbidity: observed symptom relations are explained by unobserved constructs (i.e., latent variables).
Comorbidity arises solely from relations among latent constructs, providing limited insights for identifying concrete, symptom-level intervention points.
Recent advances in psychopathology understand comorbidity through a network perspective.

Instead of considering mental disorders to be unobservable latent factors, it defines mental disorders as systems of observable symptoms (i.e., nodes) that causally interact with each other (the relations are defined as edges).

The inter-symptom interactions sustain mental disorders, and interventions should be based on understanding the connections between observed symptoms, as well as identifying the central symptoms that explain most other symptoms.

Consequently, the network perspective posits that comorbidity emerges when symptoms from one disorder causally activate and sustain symptoms from another, with cross-disorder "bridge" symptoms transmitting symptom activation across diagnostic categories (Borsboom, 2017; Borsboom & Cramer, 2013; Cramer et al., 2010; Robinaugh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Consequently, the network perspective posits that comorbidity emerges when symptoms from one disorder causally activate and sustain symptoms from another, with cross-disorder "bridge" symptoms transmitting symptom activation across diagnostic categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Borsboom, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Borsboom & Cramer, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cramer et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Robinaugh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, understanding comorbidity involves identifying the bridging symptoms that connect the symptoms of one disorder to those of another.

Due to its focus on observable features and the interactions among them, the network analysis of depression and anxiety symptoms can offer more direct insights into the onset of and the intervention for depression-anxiety comorbidity, compared to the latent variable perspective that focuses on unobservable latent variables and their relations (Borsboom, 2017; Borsboom & Cramer, 2013; Cramer et al., 2010).

text.text: Motivated by the aforementioned rationale, prior research has examined the network structure of depression and anxiety symptoms using Gaussian graphical models (GGMs) applied to cross-sectional data (Beard et al., 2016; Kaiser et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025b) and cross-lagged panel network models based on two-wave panel data (Zhang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Motivated by the aforementioned rationale, prior research has examined the network structure of depression and anxiety symptoms using Gaussian graphical models (GGMs) applied to cross-sectional data <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Beard et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kaiser et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Li et al., 2025b)</ref> and cross-lagged panel network models based on two-wave panel data <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Zhang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These studies identified essential bridge symptoms linking depression and anxiety, including psychomotor and concentration problems, restlessness (Beard et al., 2016; Kaiser et al., 2021), nervousness, guilt, (Li et al., 2025b), mood and physical retardation, somatic complaints, hypochondriasis, and diurnal variation (Zhang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These studies identified essential bridge symptoms linking depression and anxiety, including psychomotor and concentration problems, restlessness <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Beard et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kaiser et al., 2021)</ref>, nervousness, guilt, <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Li et al., 2025b)</ref>, mood and physical retardation, somatic complaints, hypochondriasis, and diurnal variation <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Zhang et al., 2024</ref>).

text.text: Yet, GGMs offer a poor estimate of causal relations (Ryan et al., 2022), and they do not reveal within-person dynamic effects (Epskamp et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Yet, GGMs offer a poor estimate of causal relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Ryan et al., 2022)</ref>, and they do not reveal within-person dynamic effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Epskamp et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Two-wave panel data do not allow models to separate within-and between-person variance.

Consequently, for cross-lagged panel network models, the estimation of within-person effects can be biased by between-person effects, leading to spurious within-person relations (Hamaker, 2023; Hamaker et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Consequently, for cross-lagged panel network models, the estimation of within-person effects can be biased by between-person effects, leading to spurious within-person relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hamaker, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hamaker et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The panel graphical vector autoregression (panelGVAR) model, by contrast, can estimate fixed effects of within-person dynamical relations between depression and anxiety symptoms while separating within-and between-person variances (Epskamp, 2020).
text.formatted: The panel graphical vector autoregression (panelGVAR) model, by contrast, can estimate fixed effects of within-person dynamical relations between depression and anxiety symptoms while separating within-and between-person variances <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Epskamp, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore aim to use this model to study the dynamics of depression and anxiety symptoms over time.

In addition, existing evidence suggests both robust and nuanced sex differences in depression, anxiety, and their comorbidity, which may have implications for how comorbidity manifests and should be treated.

Large cohort studies such as the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety have reported that women with major depressive disorder showed higher levels of comorbid anxiety and atypical features than men, suggesting potentially different underlying mechanisms and course of illness across sex groups (Schuch et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Large cohort studies such as the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety have reported that women with major depressive disorder showed higher levels of comorbid anxiety and atypical features than men, suggesting potentially different underlying mechanisms and course of illness across sex groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Schuch et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, reviews of anxiety disorders consistently find that women are about twice as likely as men to meet criteria for an anxiety disorder across the lifespan, and that comorbidity with depression is common and often more burdensome among women (McLean et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Likewise, reviews of anxiety disorders consistently find that women are about twice as likely as men to meet criteria for an anxiety disorder across the lifespan, and that comorbidity with depression is common and often more burdensome among women <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(McLean et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings indicate that depression-anxiety comorbidity is not uniform across biological sexes.
These considerations further motivated a modeling strategy that can explicitly compare network structures across sexes.

Hence, to estimate the dynamical comorbidity networks, while considering the structural differences across males and females (Du et al., 2026), we adopted a novel approach developed under the panelGVAR framework termed the invariance partial pruning (IVPP) approach (Du et al., 2026).

text.text: IVPP allows multi-group estimation of the panelGVAR model while revealing group-specific variances and the invariance of edges across groups.
The model outputs a unique network structure for each group, with some edges constrained to be equal across groups and others freely estimated within each group, based on data fit.
While designed for network comparison, IVPP is also suitable for evidence synthesis that evaluates what connections are shared across groups and what are unique to some groups.

To this end, it is well suited to investigating the dynamical relations among depression, anxiety, and transdiagnostic mechanisms to explain comorbidity, while evaluating the cross-group stability of the discovered network structures.
In this exploratory study, we seek to map the within-person temporal network linking depression and anxiety symptoms and to explore whether these dynamical networks differ between males and females.
In the networks, we also added mechanism variables that can be targeted and intervened on to inform intervention.

To do so, we will (1) fit panelGVAR models to recover within-person lagged effects among symptoms while separating within-and between-person variance, and (2) use the IVPP multi-group estimation approach to determine which edges are shared across sexes, which are group-specific, and to quantify the degree of invariance.

text.text: The method comprises three steps to determine group invariance.

The first step is a global invariance test on both the temporal and the contemporaneous networks (Hoekstra et al., 2024), where the algorithm compares a fully constrained model (M 0 ) in which both the temporal (B B B) and the contemporaneous networks (Ω Ω Ω) are constrained to be equal across groups with a free model (M 1 ) in which neither network is constrained.

text.text: The end-product of IVPP is a temporal and a contemporaneous network for each group, with some edges constrained to be equal and others freely estimated across groups.
Using the networks, we further computed the in-and out-strength centrality of each node in temporal networks and the strength centrality in contemporaneous networks.
In-strength centrality of a node is defined as the sum of all incoming edge weights, that is, the total lagged influence the node receives from all other nodes in the network (Borsboom et al., 2021).

text.text: Out-strength centrality is defined as the sum of all outgoing edge weights, reflecting the total lagged influence a node exerts on all other nodes.
Strength centrality, computed in undirected contemporaneous networks, is the sum of all edge weights incident to a node, capturing a node's overall connectivity regardless of direction.
In addition, we computed bridge centrality indices to quantify nodes' role in connecting depression, anxiety, and mechanisms (Jones et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In addition, we computed bridge centrality indices to quantify nodes' role in connecting depression, anxiety, and mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Jones et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Bridge in-strength is the sum of incoming edge weights from nodes in a different community, and bridge out-strength is the sum of outgoing edge weights to nodes in a different community.
Bridge strength is the undirected analog, defined as the sum of all edge weights connecting a node to nodes outside its own community.
We further broke down the bridge centrality measures by community pairs.
For example, the bridge out-strength of a depression symptom to anxiety indicates how much this depression symptom contributes to the transition from depression to anxiety.
Together, these indices identify nodes that may facilitate the spread of activation across symptom clusters, which is of particular clinical relevance in transdiagnostic network models.

In this longitudinal study, we examined within-person temporal and contemporaneous networks linking depression symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and transdiagnostic mechanisms during the COVID-19 pandemic, and compared these structures across biological sex using the IVPP approach.

Across four waves of data, fear ("feeling afraid as if something awful might happen") emerged as the primary temporal predictor of subsequent depressive mood and anhedonia, as well as of nervousness and restlessness.
Worry and rumination predicted later sleep disturbance.
In the contemporaneous networks, nervousness and fear were tightly connected with depressive mood.
Worry and rumination were more strongly associated with depression, whereas beliefs about the uncontrollability of worry and threat monitoring were more strongly associated with anxiety.
Overall, temporal and contemporaneous network structures were largely invariant across males and females, with only minimal, potentially spurious sex differences detected.

Bridge centrality analysis by community pairs in the temporal networks revealed the central role of fear in predicting depression in the next measurement (highest bridge out-strength to depression), through anhedonia and depressive mood (highest bridge in-strength from anxiety).
Furthermore, worry and rumination were the primary transdiagnostic mechanisms that predicted sleep disturbance in the next measurement occasion.
The contemporaneous networks showed bridges between communities within the same measurement occasion.
In the contemporaneous networks, anxiety and depression were connected through nervousness, fear, and depressive mood.
For mechanism variables, worry and rumination were more connected to depression, and beliefs about the uncontrollability of worry and threat monitoring were more connected to anxiety.
These results indicated that the main driver for depression-anxiety comorbidity could be anxiety, and depression could be a downstream disorder following persistent anxiety.
The channeling symptom was the fear that awful events might happen, which further led to anhedonia and depressive mood.
The fear was also a main predictor of other anxiety symptoms in the temporal network.
Fear and depressive mood were also the central channels between anxiety and depression in the contemporaneous networks.

However, the connection between nervous and depressive mood was stronger in the contemporaneous networks in the present study, which agreed with the findings of Beard et al. text.text: Overall, our within-person temporal analyses suggest that anxiety-related processes-particularly fear (the sense that awful events might happen)-often precede increases in depression symptoms, consistent with anxiety acting as a potential driver of short-term depression risk.
This interpretation aligns with a substantial body of longitudinal evidence.
In NESDA, anxiety preceded depression in 57% of comorbid cases, compared to only 18% in which depression came first (Lamers et al., 2011).

text.text: This asymmetry suggests that the temporal precedence of anxiety over depression may be an essential motor driving depression-anxiety comorbidity.

The temporal and contemporaneous findings suggest that fear and worry-related processes may function as dynamic "gateways" from anxiety to depression, while also providing an explanation for the dense co-occurrence of anxiety and depression symptoms at any given time point.

text.formatted: These studies were all based on GGM, and the comparisons used the network comparison test (NCT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">van Borkulo et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: One possible explanation for the sex invariance was that the present study focused on within-person effects, whereas GGM merged within-and between-person variance.
The other reason might be the conservatism of partial pruning, which relies on BIC (Du et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The other reason might be the conservatism of partial pruning, which relies on BIC <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Du et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This might be the case for comparing temporal networks.
In this test, global AIC-based tests suggested group invariance, yet only the fear self-loop showed a sex difference.
The other sex differences might not be estimated because partial pruning is conservative when the true temporal effects were weak, given the long temporal distance between the measurement periods.
The null sex difference in the contemporaneous networks might be more credible given that both AIC and BIC suggested invariance.
These findings must also be understood in light of the COVID-19 context in which the data were collected.

The pandemic introduced a combination of chronic, largely uncontrollable stressors-health threats, social restrictions, economic uncertainty, and disruptions to daily routines-that may have selectively amplified fear, worry, and threat monitoring (Hoffart et al., 2022; Magnúsdóttir et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The pandemic introduced a combination of chronic, largely uncontrollable stressors-health threats, social restrictions, economic uncertainty, and disruptions to daily routines-that may have selectively amplified fear, worry, and threat monitoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hoffart et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Magnúsdóttir et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This could partly explain why fear emerged as such a prominent temporal driver and why beliefs about the uncontrollability of worry and threat-focused attention occupied central positions in the contemporaneous networks.

At the same time, pandemic-related restrictions and lifestyle changes (for example, altered work patterns, reduced social contact, and changes in physical activity and sleep schedules) may have strengthened links between worry, rumination, and sleep disturbance.
Thus, the observed network structure may reflect, in part, how depression-anxiety comorbidity is organized under sustained external threat and uncertainty.

Although the basic mechanisms we identified (fear, perseverative negative thinking, and threat monitoring) are likely relevant beyond the pandemic (Hoffart & Johnson, 2020), the strength of specific edges-and the prominence of certain nodes-may differ in less extreme or more stable environmental conditions.
text.formatted: Although the basic mechanisms we identified (fear, perseverative negative thinking, and threat monitoring) are likely relevant beyond the pandemic <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hoffart & Johnson, 2020)</ref>, the strength of specific edges-and the prominence of certain nodes-may differ in less extreme or more stable environmental conditions.

text.text: Comparing network structure across groups is crucial for both theory and practice.

Multi-group analyses reveal whether the dynamical relations that sustain psychopathology are universal or vary systematically across subpopulations, information that cannot be recovered from pooled analyses alone.

Clinically, identifying edges that are shared across groups points to transdiagnostic targets suitable for broad interventions, whereas group-specific connections highlight the need for tailored strategies (for example, sex-sensitive assessment or intervention components).

Finally, testing for invariance helps reconcile inconsistent findings in the literature by distinguishing true heterogeneity from sampling variation or methodological differences (e.g., cross-sectional GGMs vs within-person panel models).

For these reasons, multi-group network comparison is not merely an auxiliary analysis but a central step toward translating symptom-level network insights into equitable and effective clinical practice.

When interpreting the results of the present study, one should bear in mind that VAR-based network models only represent temporal predictive relations, namely, Granger causality (Epskamp et al., 2018).
text.formatted: When interpreting the results of the present study, one should bear in mind that VAR-based network models only represent temporal predictive relations, namely, Granger causality <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Epskamp et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: One should not take predictive relations to be causal effects.
Furthermore, the measurements in this study were spaced far apart (i.e., 1.5 -2 months), so the true temporal effects were weak and difficult to detect.
Therefore, the results based on temporal networks may not generalize well to other samples.
The temporal effects estimated in the study were also weak.
In addition, the mechanism variables and anxiety symptoms are relatively stable features, whereas depression is episodic (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; Wells, 2011).
text.formatted: In addition, the mechanism variables and anxiety symptoms are relatively stable features, whereas depression is episodic <ref type="bibr">(American Psychiatric Association, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Wells, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This might attenuate the temporal variance of mechanism and anxiety variables, leading to weaker temporal links from and towards these variables.
Interpret the sex difference in contemporaneous networks with caution, as both AIC and BIC indicated invariance in the global test.
In this case, the discovered sex differences were likely false positives (Du et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In this case, the discovered sex differences were likely false positives <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Du et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the data were positively skewed, with most respondents scoring low on the symptoms and transdiagnostic mechanism items.
Furthermore, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scales are ordinal rather than continuous (Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2021).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scales are ordinal rather than continuous <ref type="bibr">(Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, there are currently no estimation methods for handling ordinal data in panelGVAR models.
This can be a promising area to pursue in the future.

In this study, missing values were handled using full-information maximum likelihood (FIML), which in general performs better than list-wise deletion, pairwise deletion, and mean substitution and yields essentially the same results as multiple imputation (MI) and complete-data maximum likelihood across a wide range of sample sizes, missingness rates, and degrees of model misfit (Schafer & Graham, 2002).
text.formatted: In this study, missing values were handled using full-information maximum likelihood (FIML), which in general performs better than list-wise deletion, pairwise deletion, and mean substitution and yields essentially the same results as multiple imputation (MI) and complete-data maximum likelihood across a wide range of sample sizes, missingness rates, and degrees of model misfit <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Schafer & Graham, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: However, FIML accuracy relies on the assumption that the data are missing-at-random (MAR).

MAR implies that, conditional on observed variables (e.g., prior-wave symptom levels and other covariates), the probability of missingness does not depend on the unobserved values themselves (Mazza & Enders, 2013).
text.formatted: MAR implies that, conditional on observed variables (e.g., prior-wave symptom levels and other covariates), the probability of missingness does not depend on the unobserved values themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Mazza & Enders, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This assumption may be violated if participants with more severe depression symptoms did not complete questionnaires during the assessment period, even after accounting for their observed symptom history.

In this case, the measurement is missing not at random (MNAR), which would underestimate symptom severity, leading to lower-than-expected scores and lower variances, and underestimating the correlational effects in this study.
Another possibility is that respondents participated only when they felt terrible and missed measurements when they felt better, because they felt it was unnecessary to join.
In this case, the sample's symptom severity would be overestimated.
However, if a person's missingness can be explained by the measurements he/she has already attended to, the data are closer to MAR, thereby enhancing the credibility of the present study.
The more missingness is explained by scores the person did not attend to, the closer it is to MNAR, thereby threatening the credibility of the present study.

Regarding the recruitment process, we aimed to reach the entire Norwegian population through a combination of the Facebook algorithm (3.6 out of 4.2 million Norwegian adults), television, radio, and newspapers (remaining 600,000).

However, the generalizability of the present sample is subject to self-selection bias (Kaźmierczak et al., 2023), which occurs when individuals volunteer for a study, leading to a non-representative sample that is often skewed toward extreme opinions or specific demographic traits (often more females and younger participants).
text.formatted: However, the generalizability of the present sample is subject to self-selection bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kaźmierczak et al., 2023)</ref>, which occurs when individuals volunteer for a study, leading to a non-representative sample that is often skewed toward extreme opinions or specific demographic traits (often more females and younger participants).

text.text: In addition, to ensure accurate estimation, we selected a limited number of nodes that did not cover all depression and anxiety symptoms.
Results may be different when additional nodes are added to the networks.
Furthermore, all data are based on self-report questionnaire data and are not clinically validated.
As such, the presence of depression or anxiety symptoms should not be interpreted as depression illness or GAD on a diagnostic level.
Future research can build on this work in several ways.
First, studies employing denser time-series designs, such as daily diary or ecological momentary assessment, are needed to capture more fine-grained temporal dynamics.

Such designs would enable examination of shorter-lag processes (hours or days rather than weeks or months), potentially revealing additional pathways by which anxiety and depression influence each other.
Second, experimental and intervention studies could test the causal status of the mechanisms highlighted here using RCT designs.

Third, applying multi-group panelGVAR and IVPP to other group comparisons (for example, clinical vs. community samples, individuals with vs. without trauma history, or different age cohorts) could clarify the extent to which the network structure of depression-anxiety comorbidity is universal versus context-specific.
Such work would also help identify which edges can be treated as broadly transdiagnostic targets and which require group-specific adaptation.
Anxiety symptoms predicted depression symptoms in the temporal comorbidity analysis.
Fear and mechanisms like worry, rumination, and beliefs about the uncontrollability of worry emerged as central drivers linking anxiety to depression symptoms contemporaneously.
These mechanisms formed a transdiagnostic core that connected anxiety and depression.
Network structures were largely invariant across males and females, suggesting that key dynamic mechanisms are shared across sexes.

These findings support network-based accounts in which comorbidity is sustained by specific symptom and mechanism interactions, and they highlight fear and perseverative negative thinking as promising targets for transdiagnostic intervention aimed at reducing the burden of co-occurring depression and anxiety.
